e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “arm,” referring to the part of the body between the shoulder and hand. It can describe a person’s physical arm or arms in ordinary bodily language. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, appearing once each in 1 Kings, Esther, and Proverbs. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines whether the arm is being mentioned as part of a person’s appearance, posture, or action.

Athanin is a personal name, preserved as “Athanin” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 1 Kings 8:2. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s specific role in that passage cannot be described further, but its basic lexical function is clear: it is a proper name used to identify a person.

This noun means a “sense”—a faculty by which a person perceives or recognizes something. It names a capacity of sensing rather than an action or event. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Jeremiah and once in 4 Maccabees. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central meaning remains a sense or perceptive faculty.

This adjective describes something unexpected—something that happens without being anticipated. It can characterize an event, circumstance, or development that catches people unprepared rather than following what they expected. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears three times, each in a different deuterocanonical book. Its central meaning remains simple: unexpected. The surrounding passage determines exactly what is unexpected in each occurrence, but the word itself points to surprise or lack of anticipation.

This Greek LXX verb describes making a clang-like sound or giving a cry. It expresses an audible outburst rather than a quiet or inward response, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the sound is understood chiefly as a clang or a cry. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, including uses in Joshua, Judges, Samuel, Psalms, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. Its central idea is a clearly heard, forceful sound.

This adjective means “both,” referring to two people or things together rather than one alone. It identifies the pair as a combined whole and can describe either persons or objects, depending on the sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 120 times, showing a regular way to refer clearly to two members of a pair. Its exact role in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to dig up or turn over the ground. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes an action of excavating earth rather than a feeling, quality, or title. It occurs twice, both in the Psalms, so its ordinary sense is clear but its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording. The word pictures ground being disturbed, opened, or removed through digging. It is therefore a practical action word referring to working beneath or into the surface of the earth.

This verb means “hear in turn”: one person listens after another has spoken, or hearing is returned in sequence. It describes taking one’s turn to hear rather than simply hearing in a general sense. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 11:2. Its exact force there depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic idea is orderly, reciprocal hearing rather than a one-sided act of listening.

This Greek LXX verb means “raise up” or “exalt”—to lift someone or something to a higher position or status. It can describe physical elevation, but it also expresses the act of honoring, promoting, or making great. The word appears 28 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Samuel, Psalms, Daniel, and Sirach. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being raised and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains lifting upward, whether literally or in rank and honor.

This Greek LXX verb means “meet” or “plead.” It can describe coming face to face with someone, while also expressing an appeal or request made to another person. Its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea concerns an encounter or an earnest address. The word occurs 51 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, showing that it is used across many narrative and legal settings.

This noun describes simplicity or frankness: an open, straightforward quality without needless complication or concealment. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation, at Job 21:23. The word’s basic sense points to an uncomplicated manner and sincere openness, though the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. It is a concise term for plainness and directness in character or conduct.

This Greek LXX verb means “renounce”: to reject or give up a person, claim, or course of action. As a verb, it describes an act of turning away rather than a thing or person itself. It occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, including three occurrences in 1 Kings and one in Jonah. The word’s precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains renouncing or abandoning something.

Aramin is a proper name, rendered as “Aramin.” It functions as a personal designation rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 9:16. The name’s exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its lexical role is simply to identify someone named Aramin.

Arēmōth, also rendered Arimoth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 20:8. Because personal names identify someone or something named in the text, its meaning is chiefly its name identity; the surrounding verse is needed to determine whom or what it designates there. The form is preserved as a name, not translated into an ordinary English description.

Arothitis is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 23:33. The available wording preserves the name as “Arōditēs; Arothitis,” so its central meaning is the person designated by that name. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word itself functions as a proper name rather than a common descriptive term.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a small shield or to the raised boss—the central protective fitting on a shield. It names a defensive piece of equipment rather than a person or action. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus, chiefly in descriptions of the priestly garments and their fittings, and once in 1 Maccabees in connection with shields. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This noun means “indecency”—conduct or a condition regarded as shamefully improper. In the Greek Old Testament, it names a kind of nakedness, dishonor, or improper behavior, while the surrounding passage determines its precise reference. It occurs 44 times in this Greek Old Testament corpus, especially in Leviticus, showing repeated use in laws addressing conduct that should not occur among God’s people. Its basic sense remains the description of something openly improper or shameful.

This adjective means “ungracious”: it describes a person or action marked by a lack of graciousness. It is a descriptive word, so it characterizes how someone behaves or how an act is regarded rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Wisdom, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name for Baithsoura, also rendered Vethsura. It identifies a named location rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 16 times, with most occurrences in 1 Maccabees and additional occurrences in 2 Maccabees and 2 Chronicles. The exact significance of the location in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

Beryl is the name of a particular stone or gemstone. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun occurs three times, and each occurrence is rendered “beryl.” It appears twice in Exodus and once in Ezekiel, showing that the word identifies a material or precious stone rather than an action, quality, or person. Its exact significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the object where it appears.

Gabe, also rendered Gave, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or place by name within the Greek Old Testament translation. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Zechariah 14:10. The supplied wording supports the name itself, but the verse text is needed to explain whom or what Gabe identifies in that passage.

Gaimele, also rendered Yemele, is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a general description, action, quality, or spiritual concept, so its meaning is the personal designation itself. This name occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Samuel 8:13 and 2 Kings 14:7. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain the person’s role in either passage.

This verb describes bearing oneself proudly or prancing, especially with a lively, confident movement. It can portray an animal displaying strength and spirited energy rather than simply walking or standing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Job 39, where the word’s basic sense concerns proud, vigorous movement. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its precise force in either occurrence, but its central idea is clear: moving or carrying oneself with visible pride and exuberance.

This Greek LXX noun means “finger,” referring to one of the digits of the hand. It normally describes a physical body part and can identify an action involving touching, placing, pointing, or applying something with a finger. The word occurs 39 times in the Greek LXX, across both the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, showing a recurring ordinary bodily meaning rather than a specialized term. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Dekmōn” or “Thekmon.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 21:37. Without the verse text or surrounding passage, its specific historical or geographical identification cannot be explained further here; the lexical sense is simply the name itself.

This Greek LXX preposition expresses movement or passage “through” something, and it can also point to a reason, meaning “because of.” It links one action, event, or circumstance to what surrounds it or causes it. The word appears 1,330 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so its precise force depends on the sentence. Its central idea is connection: moving through a medium, or acting because a particular cause or circumstance is involved.

This Greek LXX verb means “make to cease.” It expresses causing something to stop or come to an end, rather than simply describing a state of stopping. The word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament represented here, once in Leviticus and once in Hosea. Its exact force in either passage depends on what is being brought to an end by the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to give bail for someone—that is, to become responsible for fulfilling an obligation on another person’s behalf. It describes an act of guaranteeing or standing surety for someone, rather than merely offering help or making a promise. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 5:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the assumption of responsibility for another person’s debt or duty.

This verb means to destroy utterly or bring something completely to nothing. It describes total ruin rather than a minor loss or weakening. In the Greek Septuagint, it appears twice, both times in the book of Wisdom, so its meaning is clear even though it is not commonly repeated across this corpus. As a verb, it expresses the action of completely destroying something. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek noun means “dragon,” referring to a powerful serpent-like creature. In the Septuagint, it is used for such creatures in a range of passages, including accounts associated with Egypt, Job, Psalms, Jeremiah, and the book of Esther. The word occurs 35 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a dragon or great serpent-like creature.

This word is a proper name rendered “Edem” or “Ethem.” It identifies a named person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, appearing four times in Genesis and once in 2 Kings. The name’s precise referent in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context; the name itself does not provide enough information to determine that referent.

This Greek LXX adverb means “intensely” or “intensively,” describing an action carried out with strong effort, concentration, or force. It answers the question of how something is done, adding emphasis to the action rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, in Joel, Jonah, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the action and surrounding wording.

This verb means to have mercy or to have pity for someone. It describes showing compassionate concern toward a person who needs help, relief, or kindness. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used nine times, including several passages in Psalms and Proverbs, where mercy is treated as a meaningful response toward others. Its focus is not merely noticing another person’s trouble, but responding with pity toward that person. The surrounding verse determines who receives the mercy and how it is expressed.

Elisamae is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 14:7. The available wording preserves the name as “Elisamae,” so the evidence supports recognizing it as a person’s name but does not provide a separate ordinary-word definition or explain the individual’s role in that passage. Its significance in the verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage and the person’s place in that account.

This noun means “change” or “inversion”: a turning from one state, order, or condition to another. It names a change or alteration rather than describing an action by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Wisdom 14:26. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, its precise force there must be understood from that context; the basic idea remains a change or inversion.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “raise up” or “awakened.” It describes bringing someone or something up from a lower or inactive state. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to being raised, stirred into action, or awakened. The word occurs 74 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, so it is used across a broad range of passages rather than for only one special event. Its precise force in any verse comes from the surrounding context.

This noun refers to “marching out” or an “expedition”—a purposeful departure from one place toward an intended activity or destination. It describes going forth rather than simply remaining in place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, making it an uncommon word with a focused meaning. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a purposeful going out or expedition. It appears in Deuteronomy, 2 Samuel, and Micah.

This adjective describes someone or something that is on the point of death—very near dying. It expresses an immediate condition of approaching death rather than simply describing weakness or illness. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Bel and the Dragon 1:31. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, but its basic meaning is clear: death is imminent or very near. It is a descriptive word, used to characterize a person or condition facing the end of life.

This adjective describes something desirable or pleasant—something attractive, enjoyable, or valued. It can refer to possessions, surroundings, or other things regarded favorably. In the Greek Old Testament and related writings, it occurs eight times, so its basic sense is broad rather than limited to one particular kind of object. The exact shade of meaning depends on what it describes in a given verse, but the central idea remains that of something welcomed because it is pleasing or desirable.

This word means “mixed”: it describes people or things joined together without being of one kind throughout. As a noun or adjective, it can name a mixed group or describe something as mixed. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it occurs four times, so its basic sense is consistent across its uses. The surrounding verse determines what is mixed in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “delight”: to take pleasure in or be pleasing to someone. It describes an active response rather than merely naming a pleasant feeling. The word occurs 13 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented here, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, and Sirach. Its exact force—who delights, or who is pleasing—depends on the sentence and surrounding context, but its central idea remains delight or favorable pleasure.

This word refers to a daily group or division, especially an organized group assigned to serve in its turn. As a noun, it identifies a scheduled division rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 21 times, chiefly in Chronicles and Nehemiah, where organized service and assigned divisions are repeatedly mentioned. Its central idea is an orderly group arranged for regular duty. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording and context.

This adjective describes someone or something “ready to lead.” It points to a directing or governing quality, rather than merely describing strength, status, or authority in the abstract. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Psalms and once in 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains preparedness for leadership or guidance. The word functions as a description, identifying a person or quality suited to take the lead.

This noun refers to a young shoot or a young branch—the tender new growth of a plant. It names a small, developing part rather than a mature limb or trunk. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 14:4. The word’s basic meaning is botanical and concrete; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This noun means “setting; placing.” It refers to putting something in a particular position or arrangement. As a noun, it names that placement rather than describing the action with a verb. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs three times: once in 1 Kings and twice in Wisdom. The basic idea remains focused on something being set or positioned, while the surrounding verse determines what is being placed and why. It should therefore be understood as a term for placement or arrangement, without adding a more specific idea apart from its context.

This Greek LXX verb means to treasure something or store it up. It describes the act of gathering and keeping something valuable, whether the object is material or something treated as a reserve. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eleven times, across Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its use in wisdom passages fits the idea of deliberately accumulating something for a later purpose, while other occurrences may refer more generally to what is stored or gathered. The surrounding verse determines what is being treasured or stored up.

Iessia is a proper name, referring to a person named “Iessia.” It is preserved as a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezra 10:31. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, no further detail about this person or the significance of the name can be stated reliably.

Iōarib, also rendered Ioariv, is a proper name referring to a person rather than a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it appears three times: once in Ezra and twice in 1 Maccabees. Because the available information identifies the name but does not provide verse text or a further lexical definition, its precise personal or family reference must be understood from the surrounding passage in each occurrence.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Iōdiēl” or “Iothil.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 12:21. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional ordinary-language definition or explain the person’s role. Its precise significance in that passage therefore depends on the surrounding verse and account.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “bad treatment.” It refers to the experience of being treated badly, rather than naming the person who causes it. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament, including both the Old Testament books and the Deuterocanonical books. It appears across several biblical writings, showing that the idea is used as a recurring description of human experience. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and its immediate context.

The word means “heart.” It is a noun naming the heart, whether the sentence speaks of one heart or more than one. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 869 times, so it is a widely used word rather than a rare term. Its precise significance in any particular verse must be read from that verse’s surrounding context; the lexical meaning itself remains “heart.”

This verb means “grow old.” It describes becoming advanced in age, rather than naming a person or object. The wording presents aging as a process that occurs over time. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Isaiah 46:4, so its ordinary sense is clear even though the surrounding verse is not included here. Its precise force in that passage must be understood from the verse and its wider context.

This word means “afraid,” describing someone who feels fear or is frightened. It is an adjective, so it characterizes a person or group rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 36:16. The word’s basic sense remains focused on a state of fear; the surrounding verse and passage would be needed to explain what caused that fear or how it functions in that specific setting.

This Greek LXX noun means “working,” referring to the carrying out or performance of an activity or task. It names work as something being done or accomplished, rather than describing a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation represented here, at 1 Chronicles 28:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains the act of working or carrying something through.

This Greek LXX noun means “shaft,” referring to a long, rigid part of an object. It names a physical thing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Exodus and Numbers, showing a specific and concrete use rather than a broad or abstract one. The exact object meant in each passage depends on the surrounding description of that object.

This noun means “inheritance”: what is received or assigned as a lasting possession. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, it commonly refers to an inheritance connected with persons, families, or allotted portions. The word occurs 192 times in this LXX corpus, showing that inheritance is a recurring scriptural idea rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “hunt”: to pursue or seek animals as prey. It describes an action rather than a person or object, so it normally tells what someone does. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 25:27. The word’s basic sense remains simply the act of hunting; the surrounding verse supplies any further details about the person, setting, or purpose involved.

Kōph is a noun used as a name rather than an ordinary action, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Psalm 118:145, so its role is limited to that occurrence. The lexical meaning given is simply “Kōph,” with no broader English sense or additional usage recorded here. It is best understood as a designated name whose precise function depends on the surrounding psalm text.

This Greek LXX adverb means “very.” It strengthens the word or statement it accompanies, showing an especially high degree or strong intensity rather than naming a person, thing, or action by itself. In ordinary English, it functions much like “very” in phrases such as “very good” or “very greatly.” It occurs 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its basic role remains consistent across several kinds of passages.

This noun means “harbor,” a sheltered place where ships can enter, remain, or find protection. It names a physical location rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs eight times, appearing once in Psalms and seven times in the deuterocanonical books. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This is a proper name rendered as “Maachan” or “Maakhan.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, place, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs once, at 2 Chronicles 11:21. The available information establishes the name and its alternate English renderings, but does not provide the surrounding verse text needed to describe that person or the passage’s particular emphasis.

Malēsear, also rendered Malisear, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Septuagint text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Esther 1:14. Because the available text does not provide the surrounding passage here, the name itself gives identification but does not establish additional meaning, character, role, or significance for the person named.

Mariel is a proper name used to identify a person. Its lexical gloss is “Mariēl; Maril,” while the English rendering is Mariel. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles. The name appears in 1 Chronicles 5:32, 5:33, and 6:37, but the available information does not include the surrounding verse text or details about the individuals named. Therefore, its basic meaning is its function as a personal name rather than a description, action, or quality.

This word means “short sword,” referring to a bladed weapon used for close combat. It is a noun naming a physical weapon, not a general term for every kind of weapon. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 178 times, showing that this was a familiar image in accounts of warfare, danger, judgment, and personal defense. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a short sword or fighting blade.

Merob, also rendered Merov, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a general term describing an action, quality, or object, but a personal name used to distinguish one individual. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Samuel 14:49. The name itself gives the person’s designation, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that individual’s role or significance in the narrative.

e.h: Up To or As Far As
e.t: This word means “up to” or “as far as,” marking a limit, endpoint, or extent. It can function as a preposition, showing how far an action, place, time, or condition reaches, and it can also function as an adverb describing that boundary. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 50 times across 49 verses, showing regular use for expressing limits or a point reached. Its exact force in a particular passage depends on what boundary the surrounding sentence identifies.

The word means “with one testicle,” describing a person whose body has only one testicle. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, rather than a statement about character, worth, or spiritual condition. This word appears once in the LXX corpus, at Leviticus 21:20. Without the verse text and surrounding passage, its precise role there cannot be explained further; its lexical meaning remains this physical description.

This noun refers to mocking—speech or behavior that makes fun of someone in a scornful or insulting way. It names the act or character of treating another person with ridicule rather than respect. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in Sirach 33:6, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains clear: mocking is contemptuous ridicule directed toward another person.

Naphes, also rendered Nafes, is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus: once in Genesis 25:15 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:31. Because the available material gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise role in either passage must be understood from the larger context. The two spellings represent the same stated name gloss.

The word means “dwell”: to live or remain in a place. As a verb, it describes inhabiting a home or land, or continuing in a settled location. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 469 times, showing that it is a broad, ordinary word for residence rather than a term limited to one special setting. It appears from Genesis through Song of Songs. The surrounding verse determines the precise sense, but the central idea is staying or making one’s home somewhere.

This noun means “whole offering”: something presented to God in its entirety, rather than only a part or portion. It names a complete sacrificial gift and is used in the Greek Old Testament for offerings associated with worship and dedication. The word occurs ten times in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Genesis, with additional occurrences in Leviticus and Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the offering.

This word means “pickaxe,” a noun naming a tool used for digging or breaking hard ground. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 14:5. The available lexical meaning identifies the object plainly, while the exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and its list of animals. It should therefore be understood as the name of a physical implement, not as a description of a person, action, or spiritual quality.

This noun refers to an educator or disciplinarian—someone who teaches, trains, and corrects others. It can describe a person whose role includes guiding someone toward understanding or responsible conduct, not merely giving information. The word appears four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, including Hosea, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a person who instructs or disciplines.

This noun means “putting aside,” describing the act of setting something to one side or leaving it aside. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 15:32. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely what is being set aside in that occurrence, but the central idea remains the deliberate removal or placement of something apart from the immediate matter.

This noun means “lineage” or “family line”: the people connected through common family descent. It can describe a family group or a broader ancestral line, so the focus is belonging by descent rather than merely one household. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 17 times across 17 verses. Its exact scope—whether a smaller family group or an extended lineage—depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something covered, coated, or decorated with silver—something “overlaid with silver” or “silver-plated.” It identifies the material or surface treatment of an object rather than expressing an action or abstract quality. The word appears seven times in the Epistle of Jeremiah within the Greek LXX corpus, all in its first chapter. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This verb means “go around.” It describes moving around something or traveling around an area rather than simply remaining in one place. The exact sense is shaped by the sentence, but its central idea is movement around. It occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, from Joshua through Wisdom. It may describe a person or group making a circuit, or movement along or around a boundary. Its meaning is practical and directional, not a specialized spiritual term.

This verb means “sell”: to transfer something to another person in exchange for payment or value. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it is used for the act of selling property, possessions, or people. Its meaning remains direct and practical, describing a transaction or the act of giving something over for sale. It occurs 31 times in the LXX corpus, showing regular use across legal, historical, and narrative passages.

This adjective describes someone who frequently swears or is given to oaths. It portrays a person whose speech repeatedly involves solemn promises or oath-taking, rather than someone who does so only once. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, the word occurs twice, both in Sirach: once in Sirach 23:11 and once in Sirach 27:14. Its precise force in either sentence depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a person characterized by frequent swearing.

This word means “much” or “many,” describing a large amount, number, or extent. It is an adjective when it describes a person or thing, and it can function adverbially when it describes the degree or extent of an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used broadly—717 times—so its precise sense depends on what it describes: people, possessions, duration, actions, or degree. Its basic idea remains abundance or great extent, whether referring to something countable or to something measured in amount.

This Greek LXX verb means “pushed away”—to force someone or something away from a person or place. It expresses an act of rejection or removal rather than simply moving aside. The word occurs once in the Greek text of Sirach, at Sirach 13:21. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise object being pushed away and the full force of the statement must be understood from that passage’s context.

Ramia is a personal name, also rendered Rhamia. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Ezra 10:25. The available wording preserves the name itself, so its meaning is primarily identifying: it distinguishes one individual from others. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that person’s specific role or significance there.

Sarasar is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, each in a different verse: 2 Kings 19:37, Isaiah 37:38, and Zechariah 7:2. The English rendering preserves the name as “Sarasar,” and no broader lexical meaning is given. Its particular role in any one passage must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Sephi, also rendered Sefi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Samuel 19:22. The available lexical information identifies the name but does not provide an additional definition or explain the person’s identity. Its precise significance in that passage therefore comes from the surrounding verse and narrative, not from a broader abstract meaning attached to the name itself.

Siōr is a proper name, rendered “Siōr” or “Sior.” As a name, it identifies a particular named referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. This LXX word occurs twice, in Joshua 13:19 and 2 Kings 8:21. The available information identifies the name and its use as a proper noun, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely which referent is intended in each passage.

Sue is a proper name, referring to a person identified by that name rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 23:23. The available wording identifies the name as “Soue” or “Sue,” but the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, so no further detail about the person or the name’s role should be added. Its meaning is therefore best understood simply as the personal name Sue in this passage.

This Greek adjective means “stout,” describing someone or something as solidly built, thick, or robust rather than slight or delicate. It functions as a descriptive word, so its precise force depends on the noun or person it modifies. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 3:6. That single occurrence establishes its basic sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to determine exactly what is being described there.

This Greek LXX verb means to agree or to be conscious that something is so. It describes recognizing a matter inwardly and acknowledging it, whether through agreement with another person or awareness of a fact. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX material represented here, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is conscious acknowledgment or agreement.

This Greek LXX noun means “collection”—something gathered together as a group or whole. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Ecclesiastes 12:11. The word itself points to gathered material or things brought together, while the precise force of its use depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning is therefore straightforward: a collection, understood as an assembled group rather than a single item.

This Greek LXX verb means “destroy with”—to bring destruction upon someone or something together with another person or group. It describes shared or accompanying destruction rather than destruction considered entirely by itself. The word appears nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on who is being destroyed and with whom the action is connected.

This Greek LXX verb means “make to live with.” It describes causing one person to live together with another, rather than simply describing residence. The word appears three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Deuteronomy and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is bringing people into shared living. This is an LXX source-word entry and should not be treated as identical to a Greek New Testament word merely because English translations may overlap.

This Greek LXX noun means “rush,” referring to the plant named by that word. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Psalms, Jeremiah, Joel, and Micah. Its basic meaning remains concise: it identifies a rush rather than an action, quality, person, or abstract idea. The precise force of the word in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

Sōpharphak, also rendered Sofarfak, is a proper name referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 8:5. The available information identifies the name and its single occurrence, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the person’s role or significance. Its meaning in that passage must therefore be understood from the surrounding genealogy and context.

Tableth, also rendered Tavlith, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Kings 4:11. The available information identifies the person by this name but does not provide an English definition or a broader lexical sense. Its significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage, not from the name itself.

This word means “four” or “fourth,” expressing the number four or identifying something as fourth in order. It functions as a number word and can describe either a quantity or a position in a sequence. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice: once in Haggai 2:18 with the sense “four,” and once in Zechariah 8:19 with the sense “fourth.” The surrounding verse determines whether it refers to quantity or order.

gl: that in which one takes pride; pride
d: that in which one takes pride; pride

e.h: Something in Which One Takes Pride
e.t: This noun refers to that in which a person takes pride—something regarded as a source of personal honor or satisfaction. Its central meaning is “pride,” focused on the object or matter that produces pride rather than merely describing a proud attitude. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Sirach 31:3; the surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely what is being called a source of pride there.

“Waking vision” refers to a vision experienced while a person is awake, rather than a dream during sleep. This noun names that kind of visionary experience. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 15:11. The word’s basic meaning identifies the experience itself; the surrounding passage is needed to explain what the vision contains or what significance it has there. It should therefore be understood as a straightforward reference to a vision received in wakefulness.

This adjective describes someone who is still nursing at the breast—a suckling or nursing infant. It points to a very young child dependent on breast-feeding, rather than to an older child or adult. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament translation corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:27. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a suckling child or one under the breast.

gl: carry the neck high; show off
d: carry the neck high; show off

e.t: This verb means “carry the neck high; show off,” describing someone who presents himself in a visibly proud, self-important way. It focuses on outward bearing or display rather than simply identifying an inward feeling. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX, once in 2 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

Phasga is a proper name, rendered “Phasga” or “Fazga.” It functions as a name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, in Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Esther. The name appears in references including Deuteronomy 3:17, Deuteronomy 34:1, Joshua 12:3, Joshua 13:20, and Esther 9:7. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX noun means “murder” or “deed of murder,” referring to the act of unlawfully killing someone. It names the killing itself rather than a person who commits it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 1:24. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning remains a deed involving murder.

This noun means “bronze-worker” or “copper-shaper”: a person who makes or forms objects from bronze or copper. It identifies someone by skilled work with metal rather than describing the metal itself. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Wisdom 15:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a craftsman who shapes bronze or copper.

The word is a proper name, given in the lexical sense as “Chananaios; Khananeos.” It functions as a designation rather than an ordinary action, quality, or object-word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 69 times, from Genesis through Zechariah, so it is used repeatedly across the Old Testament Greek corpus. Its exact referent in any particular passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text; the word itself supplies the name, not the full situation or significance.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “snow,” referring to frozen white precipitation. It is used for snow as a visible feature of the natural world and as a description of whiteness or covering. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Job, and Kings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains snow.

This adjective describes something “soulish; psychological”—that is, something related to the soul or inner psychological life. It identifies the kind of thing being discussed rather than naming an action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:32. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning points to the inward, soul-related or psychological aspect of a person or matter.

This word describes something as beautiful—pleasing in appearance and worthy of admiration. It functions as a verb in the Greek Old Testament, expressing the quality of being beautiful rather than naming a person or object itself. In the surviving Greek Old Testament occurrences, it appears twice, both in Song of Songs, where it is rendered “beautiful.” Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains the expression of beauty.
